entry: Indian actor, film producer and politician. Khanna debuted in 1966 with *Aakhri Khat*, India's first official entry for the Academy Awards in 1967. He rose to stardom in [[Hindi]] films with the romantic musical *Aradhana* (1969), starring [[Sharmila Tagore]], and is considered the first Superstar of Hindi cinema. Khanna received the Filmfare Lifetime Achievement Award in 2005. He was elected to the Lok Sabha in 1992 as a candidate of the [[Indian National Congress]] for New Delhi. He was posthumously awarded the Padma Bhushan in 2013.

Indian actor who works predominantly in Tamil cinema. Born Shivaji Rao Gaikwad, he made his debut in K. Balachander's Tamil drama *Apoorva Raagangal* (1975) and first played antagonists before winning acclaim as a scorned lover in *Bhuvana Oru Kelvi Kuri* (1977). His action film *Billa* (1980), a remake of the [[Hindi]] film *Don*, became his biggest commercial success to that point and gave him an action hero image. He made his Hindi debut with *Andhaa Kaanoon* (1983). Later successes included *Baashha* (1995). *Chandramukhi* (2005) was for a time the highest-grossing Tamil film, and *Enthiran* (2010) and its sequel *2.0* (2018) were India's most expensive productions at the time of their release. He has appeared in about 170 films over more than five decades. The [[Government of India]] awarded him the Padma Bhushan in 2000 and the Padma Vibhushan in 2016.

Indian prime minister, 1984–1989. Gandhi, a former pilot, entered politics in 1981 after his brother's death. He became prime minister that day, after the assassination of his mother, [[Indira Gandhi]], at 40 the youngest Indian prime minister. In December 1984 the [[Indian National Congress]] won 414 of 541 seats, the largest majority to date. Controversies included the [[Bhopal disaster]] and the Bofors scandal. Sending peacekeeping troops to Sri Lanka in 1987 led to open conflict with the Liberation Tigers of Tamil Eelam (LTTE). He lost the 1989 election and was assassinated in 1991 by an LTTE suicide bomber while campaigning.

Horticultural implement consisting of a toothed bar or tines fixed to a handle, used to gather [[Hay|hay]], leaves and grass and to loosen [[Soil|soil]]. The name comes from [[Old English]] *raca*, related to Dutch *hark* and German *Rechen*, from a root meaning to scrape together. Rakes have been dated as far back as 1100 BC in China, when they had wooden tines on a wooden handle. Designs similar to modern rakes date to the 16th century, when a rake appears in *Journey to the West*. Edmund Brown patented the garden rake in 1874. In 1929 Camille J. Rocquin created a metal rake with prongs close to modern designs, and [[Plastic|plastic]] rakes came into use in the 1970s. Modern hand rakes have [[Steel|steel]], plastic or [[Bamboo|bamboo]] teeth. Leaf rakes have long, flat, L-shaped teeth, while garden rakes have stiff steel teeth for heavier work in soil and debris.

Race of usually malevolent beings in [[Hinduism]], also featured in [[Buddhism]] and [[Jainism]]. The name comes from the Sanskrit word for *demon* or *fiend*. Rakshasas are said to live on Earth and to use supernatural powers, such as shape-shifting and illusion, to disrupt Vedic sacrifices or eat humans. In the [[Ramayana]] and [[Mahabharata]], both good and evil rakshasas appear. [[Ravana]], king of Lanka, is among the best-known rakshasas. The term is also used for asuras, beings who oppose the benevolent devas.

City, capital of [[North Carolina]], U.S. Raleigh is the second most populous city in the state, after Charlotte. It is named after Sir Walter Raleigh, who founded the lost [[Roanoke Colony]]. It was an early planned city in the United States, laid out in a grid around the state capitol in Union Square. It was chosen as the state capital in 1788 and incorporated in 1792. During the [[American Civil War]] the city was spared any significant battle and fell to the Union in the war's closing days. Research Triangle Park, established in 1959, helped create thousands of jobs.

American fashion designer, philanthropist and businessman. Born Ralph Lifshitz in the [[The Bronx|Bronx]], New York City, to Jewish immigrant parents, he changed his surname at 16 because of bullying at school. He launched The Ralph Lauren Corporation in 1967 with men's ties and named his first full menswear line Polo in 1968. The Polo player emblem appeared on a women's shirt in 1971, and the company's cotton mesh Polo shirt in 1972 became emblematic of the preppy look. Lauren stepped down as chief executive in September 2015 but remains executive chairman and chief creative officer.

American lawyer and political activist. His book *Unsafe at Any Speed* (1965) criticized automobile safety, focusing on the [[General Motors]] Chevrolet Corvair, and helped lead to the National Traffic and Motor Vehicle Safety Act of 1966. A group of volunteer law students known as Nader's Raiders investigated the Federal Trade Commission, leading to its overhaul. Nader ran for president four times, in 1996 and 2000 for the Green Party and in 2004 and 2008 as an independent. There were allegations that his candidacy helped [[George W. Bush]] win a close election against [[Al Gore]]. Nader disputed this.

English composer. His works include operas, ballets, chamber music, secular and religious vocal pieces, and nine [[Symphony|symphonies]], written over sixty years. Strongly influenced by Tudor music and English folk song, his output marked a decisive break from the German-dominated style of British music in the 19th century. He was a late developer, not finding his true voice until his late thirties; studies with the French composer [[Maurice Ravel]] in 1907–1908 helped him free his music from Teutonic influences. Among his most familiar works are *Fantasia on a Theme by Thomas Tallis* (1910) and *The Lark Ascending* (1914). His ballet *Job: A Masque for Dancing* (1930) was successful and has been frequently staged. The First World War, in which he served, had a lasting emotional impact on him. He produced his last symphony months before his death at the age of 85.

American essayist, lecturer, philosopher and poet. Emerson, who went by his middle name, Waldo, led the [[Transcendentalism|transcendentalist]] movement of the mid-19th century. He set out its philosophy in his 1836 essay "Nature," which emphasized direct intuition of the divine in nature and the self over institutional religion. His essays, first delivered as lectures, include "Self-Reliance," "The Over-Soul," "Circles," "The Poet" and "Experience," with themes of individuality, freedom and the relationship between the soul and the world. Emerson supported [[Abolitionism|abolitionism]] and delivered anti-slavery speeches. He was a mentor and close friend of [[Henry David Thoreau]]. He was seen as a prescient critic of social conformity. Emerson remains among the central figures of American romanticism.

Major deity in [[Hinduism]] and the seventh avatar of [[Vishnu]]. Rama is considered an ideal man (*maryāda puruṣottama*) and the heroic protagonist of the epic [[Ramayana]]. According to the *Ramayana* attributed to Valmiki, he was born to King Dasaratha and his first wife Kausalya in [[Ayodhya]], capital of the kingdom of Kosala. He married [[Sita]] and, after a 14-year exile in the forest, assumed the Kosala throne. The kidnapping of Sita by the demon-king [[Ravana]] is a central episode, and many Hindus see Rama's life as illustrating *dharma*. Legends of Rama also appear in Jain and Buddhist texts, where he is sometimes called Pauma or Padma. Festivals mark his birth at Rama Navami, his victory at Vijayadashami and his return to Ayodhya at [[Diwali]].

King of Siam, 1782–1809, and first monarch of the Chakri dynasty. Rama I was born Thongduang and became Siam's most powerful military leader while serving King Taksin in wars against the Burmese [[Konbaung dynasty]]. In 1782 he deposed Taksin and took the throne, founding the Rattanakosin Kingdom and making [[Bangkok]] its capital. His reign revived Siamese culture after the collapse of the Siamese kingdom in 1767, and he established a new purified Buddhist sect that tied Buddhism closely to the monarchy. The most famous event of his reign was the Burmese–Siamese War (1785–1786), the last major Burmese assault on Siam. His reign also began a "Golden Age of Culture," and the Thai *Ramakien* adapted the Indian [[Ramayana]].

Ninth month of the [[Islamic calendar]], observed by Muslims as a month of [[Fasting|fasting]]. Believers also devote the month to communal prayer, reflection, study of the [[Quran]] and charity. The Quran is believed to have been revealed to the prophet [[Muhammad]] during Ramadan, and the observance is one of the [[Five Pillars of Islam|five pillars of Islam]]. Fasting from dawn to sunset is obligatory for Muslims who have reached puberty, except those who are ill, traveling, elderly, breastfeeding, pregnant or menstruating. The predawn meal is *suhur*, and the evening meal that ends the fast is *iftar*. The month lasts 29 or 30 days, from one sighting of the crescent moon to the next.

Indian Hindu mystic. Born in Kamarpukur, Bengal, Ramakrishna became a temple priest at the Dakshineshwar Kali Temple in [[Kolkata|Calcutta]] around the age of twenty. He was a devotee of the goddess Kali but also practiced [[Vaishnavism]], Tantric Shaktism, Advaita Vedanta, [[Christianity]] and Sufi Islam. His parable-based teachings stressed the essential unity of religions, describing them as "so many paths to reach one and the same goal." He married Sarada Devi in 1859, a marriage that was never consummated, and was initiated into sannyasa in 1865. He attracted disciples and founded the monastic Ramakrishna Order, emphasizing direct spiritual experience over scriptural injunctions. He died of throat cancer, and his chief disciple, [[Swami Vivekananda]], continued and expanded his mission in India and the West.

City in the central [[West Bank]], administrative capital of the Palestinian Authority. It is situated on the Judaean Mountains, north of [[Jerusalem]]. In the 14th century it was a mixed Christian and Muslim village, resettled in the early 16th century first by Muslims and then by Christians. Ramallah was annexed by Transjordan after the [[1948 Arab–Israeli War]], and Israel captured it in the [[Six-Day War]] in 1967. Since the 1995 [[Oslo Accords]], the Palestinian Authority has governed it, and it houses the Mukataa and Palestinian Legislative Council. Muslims became a majority by 2017, though Christians remain a significant minority.

Spectroscopic technique typically used to determine vibrational modes of [[Molecule|molecules]]. Named after the physicist [[C. V. Raman]], it relies on inelastic scattering of photons, known as Raman scattering, usually from a laser. Because Raman scattering is weak, the intense laser light scattered elastically, known as [[Rayleigh scattering]], must be filtered out. The technique provides a structural fingerprint by which molecules can be identified. Inelastic scattering was predicted by Adolf Smekal in 1923 but was not observed in practice until 1928.

Indian Hindu sage. Born Venkataraman Iyer in Tiruchuli, [[Tamil Nadu]], he is regarded by followers as a *jivanmukta*, or liberated being. At 16, in 1896, he had a "death-experience," and six weeks later he left his uncle's home in [[Madurai]] for the sacred hill of Arunachala, where he remained for the rest of his life. His followers regarded him as an avatar of [[Shiva]], and an ashram grew up around him, where visitors received instruction through silent presence and questions. He recommended self-enquiry as the principal means to remove ignorance, together with *bhakti* or surrender to the Self. His teachings have been popularized in the West since the 1930s.

Indian Hindu philosopher, guru and social reformer. Ramanuja is one of the most important exponents of the Sri Vaishnavism tradition in [[Hinduism]]. He was the chief proponent of *Vishishtadvaita* (qualified non-dualism), a school of [[Vedanta]] that competed with the dualism of Madhvacharya and the non-dualism of Adi Shankara. Together the three are the most influential Vedantic philosophies of the second millennium. He presented devotion to a personal God, [[Vishnu]], as a means to spiritual liberation, and his thought was influential in the Bhakti movement. In his doctrine, the individual self retains its distinct existence and agency in liberation, realizing communion with [[Brahman]] through devotional service rather than ontological identity. He wrote commentaries on the Brahma Sutras and the [[Bhagavad Gita]]. Born into a Tamil Brahmin family in Sriperumbudur, near [[Chennai]], he studied under Yādava Prakāśa before the two separated.

Indian [[Hindi]]-language epic television series. Created, written and directed by Ramanand Sagar, it is based on the [[Ramayana]] and originally aired on DD National in 1987–1988. It draws mainly on Valmiki's *Ramayana* and Tulsidas's *Ramcharitmanas*. During its run it became the most watched television series in the world, with a viewership of 82 percent. According to the [[BBC]], it has been viewed by over 650 million viewers. Reruns during the 2020 coronavirus lockdown drew 77 million viewers on 16 April 2020.

Ancient Sanskrit epic poem, traditionally attributed to [[Valmiki]]. The Ramayana is one of the two great epics of [[Hinduism]], with the [[Mahabharata]], and has nearly 24,000 verses in seven books. It narrates the life of [[Rama]], the seventh avatar of Vishnu and prince of Ayodhya. Rama accepts a fourteen-year exile in the forest, during which [[Sita]], his wife, is abducted by [[Ravana]], king of Lanka. [[Hanuman]] becomes Rama's greatest devotee, and Rama wins the battle against Ravana and returns to Ayodhya to be crowned king. Scholarly estimates for its oral origins range from the 8th–5th to the 5th–4th century BCE. The epic strongly influenced later Sanskrit poetry and Hindu culture, and its ideal of *Rāmarājya*, a utopian state where Rama is king, reflects its emphasis on virtue.

Medium-sized tropical tree of the family Sapindaceae, and its edible fruit. Known scientifically as *Nephelium lappaceum*, the tree is native to Southeast Asia, with its center of diversity in [[Indonesia]]. The sweet fruit has a hairy, leathery rind, and its name derives from the Malay *rambut*, meaning hair. It is closely related to other tropical fruits, including the [[Lychee|lychee]], longan and pulasan. Around the 13th to 15th centuries, Arab traders introduced rambutan to [[Zanzibar]] and East Africa. Canned rambutan in syrup is 78% water and supplies 82 calories per 100 g.

Japanese noodle dish with Chinese roots. Chinese-style alkaline wheat noodles are served in hot broth, commonly flavored with soy sauce or miso and topped with sliced pork and nori. The dish developed in [[Yokohama]] Chinatown in the late 19th century and was largely confined to the Chinese community until after World War II. Its name is borrowed from the Chinese *lamian*, meaning pulled noodles. Instant ramen, invented by Momofuku Ando in 1958, further popularized the dish. Ramen is considered a national dish of Japan, with regional styles such as tonkotsu in [[Kyushu]] and miso in [[Hokkaido]].

[[Pharaoh]] of [[Ancient Egypt|ancient Egypt]], second ruler of the Twentieth Dynasty. He is considered the last pharaoh of the New Kingdom to wield substantial power. Some scholars date his reign to 1185–1154 BC. His long reign coincided with the decline of Egyptian political and economic power, linked to foreign invasions and internal economic problems. He defeated the [[Sea Peoples]] in two battles, the Battle of Djahy on land and the Battle of the Delta at the mouth of the Nile, which saved Egypt from a collapse that overtook many empires of the [[Late Bronze Age collapse|Late Bronze Age]]. The damage of the invasions nonetheless took a toll on Egypt. He built one of the largest mortuary temples at western Thebes, now called Medinet Habu. He was assassinated in a harem conspiracy led by his secondary wife Tiye and her eldest son Pentawere, and he was succeeded by his son Ramesses IV.

King of Sukhothai, 1279–1298. Ramkhamhaeng, the third king of the Phra Ruang dynasty, reigned during the most prosperous era of the Sukhothai Kingdom in what is now [[Thailand]]. At 19 he took part in his father's campaign to capture Sukhothai from the [[Khmer Empire]], which established the kingdom's independence. He sent embassies to Yuan China from 1282 to 1323 and imported techniques for making the ceramics now known as Sangkhalok ceramic ware. Thai history credits him with creating the Thai alphabet, drawing on the Khmer, Sanskrit, [[Pali]] and Grantha alphabets. He also firmly established [[Theravada]] Buddhism as the state religion. It is speculated that his kingdom extended as far as Lampang, Phrae and Nan in the north.

German metal band. Rammstein is a Neue Deutsche Härte band formed in [[Berlin]] in 1994, and its lineup has remained unchanged. Till Lindemann writes and sings the lyrics. Its debut album, *Herzeleid* (1995), initially sold poorly but gained popularity through live performances. The second album, *Sehnsucht* (1997), debuted at No. 1 in Germany. The band is considered the most successful German-language band of all time. Its album *Liebe ist für alle da* was placed on the index of the German Federal Review Board for Media Harmful to Minors because of its song "Ich tu dir weh."
